checks.name: 00-opening: diagram and explanation do not overlap

detail.title: How Tonga lost its connection
detail.body: An eruption. A damaged cable. Weeks without normal internet access. Follow the connection that made Tonga vulnerable, the evidence of its failure, and the work that brought service back.
detail.takeaway: A guided explanation in about two minutes. Pause and inspect any claim.

checks.name: 01-chapter: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter 1 exposes explanation, takeaway and question

detail.title: One cable across an ocean
detail.body: Tonga’s international submarine cable connected the country to Fiji and onward to global networks. ITU described it as Tonga’s only international cable. Follow that long connection: a failure offshore could interrupt communications across the islands, far beyond the place where the cable was damaged.
detail.takeaway: A distant physical connection supported everyday digital life.
detail.question: Why this cable mattered

checks.name: 02-chapter: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter 2 exposes explanation, takeaway and question

detail.title: The connection falls silent
detail.body: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai erupted. Cable faults were reported, and by about 05:30 UTC Cloudflare saw almost no traffic from Tonga’s two main internet providers. The network collapse is visible in those measurements; the exact underwater break locations are not established by this account.
detail.takeaway: Reported cable damage accompanied an observed network collapse.
detail.question: Show the outage evidence

checks.name: Back returns to the preceding chapter
Evidence pauses progression without losing chapter
03-chapter: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter 3 exposes explanation, takeaway and question

detail.title: The timeline has a gap
detail.body: Traffic was already declining around 03:00 UTC. NASA places the main explosion at 04:14; near-zero traffic followed by 05:30. That ordering matters. These sources show a major disruption, but they do not explain why the first decline began before the main explosion.
detail.takeaway: The first decline predates the main explosion. Its cause remains unresolved.
detail.question: Compare the source accounts

checks.name: 06-question-answer: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter question answers in place and pauses the explanation
04-chapter: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter 4 exposes explanation, takeaway and question

detail.title: A lifeline while repairs continued
detail.body: Satellite assistance gave essential services another way to communicate. ITU documented a weather-service terminal at Fuaʻamotu Airport realigned to reach an Intelsat satellite. Temporary bandwidth, equipment and satellite phones supported the response while the damaged submarine connection still needed repair.
detail.takeaway: Emergency access supported essential services; it did not mean full recovery.
detail.question: Read the emergency response

checks.name: 05-chapter: diagram and explanation do not overlap
Chapter 5 exposes explanation, takeaway and question

detail.title: Back online was not everyone
detail.body: Cloudflare saw traffic climb toward earlier levels shortly after midnight on February 22. Digicel announced restored service on Tongatapu and Eua after cable repairs. But the domestic cable to outer islands still needed work. The main link’s return was a milestone, not the end for everyone.
detail.takeaway: The international connection returned before domestic recovery was complete.
detail.question: Check what recovered

checks.name: 07-conclusion: diagram and explanation do not overlap

detail.title: What this crisis reveals
detail.body: Tonga’s connection depended on infrastructure far beyond the shoreline. Emergency satellite access supported essential services while cable repairs restored the main link. Restoring the main link did not establish recovery for every island—and the evidence still leaves gaps.
detail.takeaway: A repaired international link did not establish recovery for every island.
